name: Reactionary feminism
summary: Reactionary feminism, a term Mary Harrington coined and set out in Feminism Against Progress, holds that sex differences are real, irreducible and politically important, and that women are harmed by a technological, market-driven 'progress' that treats the body as raw material. It favours a feminism of care and interdependence: marriage, motherhood valued, single-sex spaces, 'rewilding sex' away from the Pill, and resistance to transhumanism and gender ideology, usually through culture rather than law.
scope: Represents the doctrine as set out by Mary Harrington, who named it, in Feminism Against Progress (2023) and her interviews and essays, with Louise Perry named alongside her by reviewers (Jensen; DeSanctis) as a parallel critic of the sexual revolution. The defining sources here are Harrington's own interviews and addresses and reviews quoting the book; the book itself was not obtained, and Perry's own works were not opened, so answers rest on Harrington. It excludes tradwife influencers, conservative women generally and trans-exclusionary radical feminism as such.

accelerate-technology.rationale: She says society must move on from 'fearing or seeking to disrupt what is normal' and denies that dissolving institutions in the name of progress is a mandate.

equal-conscription.rationale: She argues some work, 'paradigmatically childcare and the military', should be segregated by sex.

exclude-trans-women-women-only-spaces.rationale: She argues for single-sex spaces for both sexes and says denying male spaces undermines the case for women's; her sex-realism treats trans women as male.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: She holds that sex cannot be changed, calls gender ideology a 'magical thinking' break from material sex, and welcomes the two-sexes executive order and British victories as 'great news'.

gender-social-construct.rationale: She holds sex differences are real and irreducible, yet describes the homemaker/breadwinner 'traditional gender roles' as distinctively modern and says what the differences mean in practice varies with the technological and cultural environment.

human-decline-since-golden-age.rationale: She states directly: 'I don't believe in progress, but I don't believe in decline either.'

human-enhancement.rationale: She calls transhumanism's project of mastering the body 'profoundly anti-women' and wants to resist it, though the sources show a cultural rather than a legal rejection.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: She says on some metrics life is 'a great deal better' and on others much has been lost, while holding that the industrial era's settlement is gone; the evidence points both ways but not to 'disaster'.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Her reviewer reports she wants marriage understood as an indissoluble 'covenant rather than a contract'.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: She grounds feminism in the sexed category of women whose interests are 'sometimes distinct', yet says the idea that women share one universal set of interests is weaponised on behalf of the market.

open-borders.rationale: She lists refusal to enforce national borders among the boundary-dissolving habits of the progressive order she criticises.

premarital-sex.rationale: She wants sex made 'consequential again', criticises the Pill for making casual sex easy, and values marriage; she hopes for cultural rather than legal rejection of casual sex.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: She says a nation should defend its culture's priorities and the sensibilities of distinct peoples against internationalist pressure, while doubting nation-states will last.

rehabilitation.rationale: She criticises progressive ideologies that 'refuse to set boundaries, punish criminals' or enforce standards.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: She says the women's movement fails to appreciate that 'we owe to Christianity our belief that women are people at all', while granting some biblically grounded misogyny exists.

restore-past-order.rationale: She says she is no conservative and that it is 'not meaningful to say that things used to be better in the past and we need to get back', though she also rejects progress.

self-ownership.rationale: She rejects self-ownership and 'bodily autonomy' as the basis for women's personhood, arguing it cannot account for motherhood and leads to selling the body, and urges valuing interdependence.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Harrington says Butler's claim that even embodied sex is rhetorically constructed 'is not actually true' and that 'Human nature is real'; reactionary feminism begins from sex differences being 'real, irreducible'.

shared-human-nature.rationale: She states that 'Human nature is real', opposes remodelling bodies at will, and grounds reactionary feminism in what makes people human together.

socialized-care.rationale: In the book she links nursery-based childcare to 'suffocating care' by a third-party pseudo-parent and wants care kept within families and the home economy.

spiritual-nature.rationale: She says defending women means defending people as 'bodies and souls together' and that moral and political matters cannot be separated.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: She rejects faith in progress, says technological advance does not improve morals or safety, and holds that technology brings new exploitation for many.

traditional-family.rationale: She advises marriage and a two-parent household as the best support for women and children, and calls marriage a commitment beyond romance, though she rejects the industrial-era 'traditional' homemaker model as modern.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: She calls the nineteenth-century inability of wives to divorce or keep earnings a real problem that made the feminism of freedom legitimate, yet also favours an indissoluble marriage covenant.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: She calls the feminists who sought women's legal agency (keeping earnings, divorce, property) legitimate, and her reviewer says she argues women's property rights are good.

women-suffrage.rationale: Her reviewer reports that in the book she argues women's political and property rights have been a good thing.

missingStatements.text: Human beings are fundamentally interdependent rather than autonomous.
missingStatements.rationale: Harrington argues that autonomy cannot account for motherhood and that people need one another, so an account of the person must begin from dependence.

quotes.text: “Autonomy” is radically incompatible with motherhood. When you have a dependent baby to care for you need a richer account of the good.

notes: Sources are one author's interviews and address plus reviews; Feminism Against Progress and Perry's book were not obtained, and the Kay article (Feminist Media Studies 2024) and The Atlantic and Telegraph pieces were blocked and not used. Themes searched in new sources beyond the statement pass: law and abortion (reviewers report no ban sought), sex work and surrogacy, childcare and work, marriage and divorce, nations and international bodies, immigration and borders, trans policy, markets and capitalism. The record states almost nothing on economics, government structure, foreign policy, ecology or most of the economy and government themes, so those stay null. Strands: Harrington says she is not a conservative, and Christian reviewers (Jensen, DeSanctis) read her through their own faith; those readings are not counted.

keyFigures.role: Coined the term and wrote Feminism Against Progress (2023).
keyFigures.quote: The dust jacket on the British edition of Mary Harrington’s Feminism Against Progress features Artemis, Greek goddess of apparent paradoxes. She is the hunter, but also the hunted; she stands for chastity, but also childbirth. It’s a fitting image for a book that advocates “reactionary feminism,”
